interactions.label: A 72-year-old man presents with a tender, tense, irreducible right inguinal hern

params.question: A 72-year-old man presents with a tender, tense, irreducible right inguinal hernia, repeated vomiting, and absolute constipation. He is haemodynamically stable after initial resuscitation. What is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen and pelvis to confirm strangulation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In a clinically obvious strangulated hernia, ordering CT to confirm the diagnosis wastes critical time while trapped bowel is losing its blood supply. Imaging is reserved for equivocal cases such as an obese patient with a difficult groin examination.

answers.text: Plain abdominal X-ray to confirm bowel obstruction before deciding on surgery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Although X-ray can confirm obstruction, it does not change management here. The clinical picture is unambiguous: a strangulated hernia requires emergency surgery. Imaging delays compromise bowel viability.

A tense, tender, irreducible hernia with vomiting and absolute constipation is a clinical diagnosis. The patient needs the operating theatre after resuscitation, not a scanner — imaging earns its place only in equivocal cases.

answers.text: Bedside ultrasound of the groin to assess bowel viability before proceeding

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While ultrasound can assess bowel viability, a clinically obvious strangulated hernia with obstruction features demands theatre, not imaging. Every minute of delay risks irreversible bowel ischaemia.

overallFeedback.feedback: A clinically obvious strangulated hernia needs the operating theatre, not a scanner. Trapped bowel loses its blood supply by the minute, and imaging to confirm the obvious wastes that critical time.
Correct. A strangulated hernia with clear obstruction features is a clinical diagnosis requiring emergency surgery — the key lesson is knowing when NOT to scan.

interactions.label: On a non-contrast CT head, a hyperdense biconvex collection is seen in the tempo

params.question: On a non-contrast CT head, a hyperdense biconvex collection is seen in the temporal region. It does not cross the adjacent suture line. Which of the following best explains this imaging appearance?

answers.text: Torn bridging veins causing blood to spread freely beneath the dura

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Torn bridging veins produce subdural haematomas, which are crescentic in shape, cross suture lines freely, and stop only at the midline falx. The biconvex shape seen here rules out a subdural collection.

answers.text: Rupture of the middle meningeal artery with blood limited by dural attachment at sutures

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The dura adheres tightly at each suture line. When the middle meningeal artery ruptures — typically from a pterion fracture — arterial blood strips the dura off the inner table but cannot cross sutures, producing the classic biconvex (lens-shaped) extradural haematoma.

answers.text: Cortical contusion with haemorrhage tracking beneath the calvarium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cerebral contusions appear as patchy hyperdense foci within the brain parenchyma, classically at the frontal and temporal poles from coup–contrecoup forces. They do not form biconvex extra-axial collections.

answers.text: Venous sinus thrombosis causing focal blood accumulation in the temporal fossa

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Venous sinus thrombosis produces a hyperdense sinus sign and may lead to secondary venous infarction, not a biconvex extra-axial collection limited by suture lines.

overallFeedback.feedback: A biconvex (lens-shaped) hyperdense collection limited by suture lines is the classic extradural haematoma. The dura binds tightly at each suture, so arterial blood from a ruptured middle meningeal artery cannot cross them — unlike subdural blood, which is crescentic and crosses sutures freely.

Correct. The biconvex shape and suture-line limitation are the hallmarks of an extradural haematoma, caused by middle meningeal artery rupture — the single most clinically useful distinction in trauma neuroimaging.

interactions.label: On contrast-enhanced CT of a patient with strangulated hernia, a trapped loop of

params.question: On contrast-enhanced CT of a patient with strangulated hernia, a trapped loop of bowel is identified. Which imaging finding most reliably indicates that the bowel is non-viable and will require resection?

answers.text: Dilatation of the proximal bowel to more than 4 centimetres

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Proximal bowel dilatation confirms mechanical obstruction but says nothing about the viability of the trapped loop itself. The key sign of non-viability is whether the bowel wall takes up contrast.

answers.text: Presence of free fluid surrounding the trapped loop

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Free fluid indicates inflammation or transudation and accompanies many causes of obstruction. It does not reliably distinguish viable from non-viable bowel — the definitive discriminator is bowel-wall enhancement.

answers.text: Thickening of the bowel wall beyond 5 millimetres

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bowel-wall thickening can result from oedema in simple obstruction and does not reliably confirm ischaemia. Absent wall enhancement, not wall thickness alone, is the critical sign of non-viability.

Bowel-wall enhancement is the single most important sign of viability on contrast CT. Viable bowel brightens with contrast; ischaemic bowel does not. Absent enhancement means non-viable bowel that will require resection.

overallFeedback.feedback: Bowel-wall enhancement on contrast CT is the single most important sign of viability. Viable bowel brightens with contrast, while ischaemic bowel fails to enhance — that absence of enhancement means non-viable bowel requiring resection.
Correct. Viable bowel enhances with contrast; ischaemic bowel does not. Absent bowel-wall enhancement is the most reliable indicator that the trapped bowel is dead and resection is necessary.

interactions.label: A CT abdomen of a patient with suspected appendicitis shows a well-defined 4 cm

params.question: A CT abdomen of a patient with suspected appendicitis shows a well-defined 4 cm peri-appendiceal abscess with no free intraperitoneal air. Which management pathway do these imaging findings support?

answers.text: Immediate appendicectomy via an open or laparoscopic approach

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: When appendicitis has progressed to a contained abscess, immediate surgery risks disrupting the walled-off infection and causing peritoneal contamination. The imaging finding changes the plan from prompt surgery to a staged approach.

Emergency laparotomy is reserved for free perforation with generalised peritonitis — there would be free intraperitoneal air and diffuse contamination. A contained abscess without free air is managed with a staged approach.

answers.text: Intravenous antibiotics, percutaneous drainage if needed, then interval appendicectomy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A contained peri-appendiceal abscess changes the plan: intravenous antibiotics first, image-guided percutaneous drainage if needed, then interval appendicectomy weeks later. This is imaging directly guiding the management pathway.

answers.text: Conservative management with oral antibiotics and outpatient follow-up

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A 4 cm peri-appendiceal abscess requires intravenous antibiotics and potential percutaneous drainage under inpatient care, not outpatient oral antibiotics. The abscess needs active management before definitive surgery.

overallFeedback.feedback: A contained peri-appendiceal abscess changes the management pathway: intravenous antibiotics, percutaneous drainage if needed, then interval appendicectomy weeks later. The CT finding does not just describe an abscess — it tells the surgeon to stage the operation.

Correct. A contained abscess changes the management from immediate appendicectomy to a staged approach — exactly the principle that imaging answers the surgeon's management question, not just labels a finding.
